name: Banana peel teeth whitening

lead: Banana peel whitening means rubbing the inside of a banana peel on the teeth for a few minutes, hoping to brighten them. It is passed around as a cheap, natural home remedy and an alternative to peroxide whitening.

Proponents say compounds or minerals in the peel lift stains. No published clinical studies of the practice were found, and established whitening works mainly by peroxide breaking down pigment molecules.

paras: People rub the inner side of a peel over the teeth for a few minutes a day, then brush and rinse. It is used as a daily habit alongside normal brushing and often over a couple of weeks. Users share before-and-after results informally.
No specific harms from the practice were found in the sources reviewed. Dentists generally note that tooth stains differ in type and that surface stains are usually handled by professional cleaning.

angle.text: People rub the inside of a banana peel on their teeth for a few minutes a day as a low-cost natural whitener, believing minerals in the peel lift stain. It is a simple daily habit shared in appearance and oral-care circles. No clinical studies of it were found.

lead: Banana peel teeth whitening is a home practice in which the inside of a banana peel is rubbed on the teeth, usually for a few minutes a day, to make them look whiter and brighter. People share it as a low-cost, natural alternative to peroxide whitening and discuss it in appearance and oral-care circles as a folk remedy.

Professional and over-the-counter whitening relies mainly on peroxide compounds that break down pigment molecules, and dental sources distinguish extrinsic stain on the tooth surface from intrinsic stain inside the tooth.[1] Banana peel is not listed as a whitening agent in encyclopedic descriptions of the fruit.[2]

Laboratory studies on extracted or bovine teeth have tested banana peel directly. A 2026 in vitro study found a banana peel herbal toothpaste gave the largest color change reduction among three agents on stained extracted incisors, while a 2025 study and a 2022 study found banana peel less effective than carbamide peroxide.[3][4][5] No clinical trials in people were found.
infobox: Typically the cost of a banana

paras: Practitioners describe rubbing the white inner side of a ripe banana peel against the teeth, often for around five minutes. Proponents attribute the effect to minerals or other compounds in the peel. The peel is the protective outer layer of the fruit and is usually discarded after the fruit is eaten.[2]

A 2026 in vitro study used 60 extracted incisors stained with iron medication or pomegranate juice and compared three whitening modalities; the banana peel herbal toothpaste gave the largest reduction in color change, ahead of whitening strips and gel, and pomegranate stains were more reversible than iron stains.[3]

A 2025 in vitro study on 64 human molars in artificial saliva compared pineapple, banana peel (rubbed for 5 minutes), 10% carbamide peroxide and a negative control. Color change was highest with carbamide peroxide, followed by pineapple, banana peel and control, and the authors judged the natural options less effective than the at-home whitener.[4]

A 2022 study on 70 bovine enamel fragments compared conventional toothpaste, charcoal, turmeric, banana peel and 16% carbamide peroxide; carbamide peroxide produced the greatest color change and reduced enamel microhardness, and the authors concluded the popular natural products were not efficient for whitening.[5]

Dental sources describe stains as intrinsic (inside the tooth) or extrinsic (on the surface), with peroxide agents aimed mainly at intrinsic stains and professional cleaning at surface stains.[1] Dental erosion, an irreversible loss of tooth structure from non-bacterial acids, is associated with acidic foods and drinks and frequent exposure.[6] The 2022 study reported that carbamide peroxide lowered enamel microhardness while banana peel's effect on gloss was smaller than some other products.[5] No reports of harm specific to banana peel use were found.

No studies found in people. Laboratory work consists of the three in vitro studies above; two found banana peel less effective than carbamide peroxide, and one found a banana peel toothpaste outperformed whitening strips and gel on iron- and pomegranate-stained teeth.[3][4][5] Studies of tooth whitening more broadly concern peroxide-based products, with tooth sensitivity the most common side effect.[1]
